messages.subject: problem with a simple correlation model
parts:
I'm again using this book and trying to implement their Bugs models to Stan: https://webfiles.uci.edu/mdlee/BB_Free.pdf. The model is on page 63. Graphical model and Bugs model code can be found there. 

I think that I don't have any mistake in the model. But the sampling gets too autocorrelated and the samples also seems to be a bit different on the average. Look at the attached pdf. Negative correlation is more probable in Stan compared to Jags (same with WinBugs) and the difference is also visible in higher values of "r". 

I have tried many things to solve it, but the results were always unstable and if stable, then a bit different from Jags.
It starts to be problematic when I input higher "sigmaerror". When I put = c(.03,1), sampling is neat.
What I've noticed is that sigma[2] is twice higher on average in Stan and is having problem reaching lower values. 

Any idea what goes wrong? I never understand why these autocorrelations are happening and what triggers it. 

Stan Code:  

# clears workspace: 
rm(list=ls(all=TRUE)) 

library(rstan)

model <- "
# Pearson Correlation With Uncertainty in Measurement
data{ 
  int<lower=0> n;
  vector[2] x[n];
  vector[2] sigmaerror;
}
parameters{
  vector[2] mu;
  vector<lower=0>[2] lambda;
  real<lower=-1,upper=1> r;
  vector[2] y[n];
} 
transformed parameters{
  vector<lower=0>[2] sigma;
  cov_matrix[2] T;

  #Reparameterization
  sigma[1] <- 1 / sqrt(lambda[1]);
  sigma[2] <- 1 / sqrt(lambda[2]);
  T[1,1] <- 1 / lambda[1];
  T[1,2] <- r * sigma[1] * sigma[2];
  T[2,1] <- r * sigma[1] * sigma[2];
  T[2,2] <- 1 / lambda[2];
}
model{
  # Priors
  mu ~ normal(0,sqrt(1000));
  lambda ~ gamma(.001,.001);
  r ~ uniform(-1,1);

  # Data
  for (i in 1:n){
    y[i] ~ multi_normal(mu,T);
    for (j in 1:2){
      x[i,j] ~ normal(y[i,j],sigmaerror[j]);
    }
  }
}"

x <- matrix(c(.8, 102,
              1,  98,
             .5, 100,
             .9, 105,
             .7, 103, 
             .4, 110,
            1.2,  99,
            1.4,  87,
             .6, 113, 
            1.1,  89,
            1.3,  93), nrow=11,ncol=2,byrow=T) 

n <- nrow(x) # number of people/units measured

sigmaerror = c(0.03, 10)

data <- list(x=x, n=n, sigmaerror=sigmaerror) # to be passed on to Stan

samples <- stan(model_code = model, data = data,# init=myinits,
               iter = 5000, chains = 3)           

print (samples)


Thank you for any help.

Martin

Martin:
I'm not sure, but these dgamma(.001,.001) priors can create serious problems; see here:
http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/taumain.pdf
I don't know what's going on in this particular example, but this is not a model I'd ever want to be fitting.
Do you get the same problem if you use uniform priors on sigma1 and sigma2?  Also, for this model, we might prefer the LKJ parameterization of the covariance matrix.  Stan has various covariance models so you can model that matrix directly, no need for the T[1,1], T[2,1], etc. stuff.
Andrew

parts:
On 9/7/13 7:00 PM, Martin ï¿½mï¿½ra wrote:
> Yes, I've tried using uniform prior for sigma1 (0,2) and sigma2 (0,50), but it doesn't help.
> Do you think LKJ parameterization would help? I'll try it tomorrow, seems complicated.

I don't think it'll help control the sampling. But you'll
want to do something like this for higher dimensions than 2.

I reparameterized your model with a uniform prior for scale
instead of your vague inverse gamma for precision.

I also rewrote it to be a bit more efficient. It may not be
ideal for pedagogical purposes --- we struggle with the balance
between writing clear and writing fast models (ideally, Stan would be
smart enough to turn the former into the latter!).

It looks like the model mixes well and produces posterior draws for
r (correlation) that look like the values I see in figure 5.4.
And it's recovering reasonable mu values. I'm not seeing the
wild multimodal posterior densities you plotted.

Where did your inputs come from and did they match the inputs
that generated fig 5.4 in the notes? From the text,
it looks like

sigmaerror = c(0.03,1)

was the input. But in your code, it was

sigmaerror = c(0.03,10).

Even if I use more error, I recover roughly the same values, though effective
sample size is quite a bit lower per iteration.

You also have this:

mu ~ normal(0,sqrt(1000));

which is an informative prior on the scale you're at,
because the posterior mean of mu[2] is 98, whereas sqrt(1000)
is only 32, and there are only 12 noisy data points!

For instance, changing it to

mu ~ normal(0,sqrt(10000));

raises the posterior mean estimate of mu[2] from 98 to 100.

This prior may also not be interacting well with the noise model that has
scale sd = 10 in the more extreme parameterization.

In general, it can be problematic when you're estimating values
near boundaries. What happens in Stan is that we logit transform
bounded values (and then scale and translate them). Values near
boundaries on (-1,1) represent logit values near -infinity or +infinity,
which can be difficult numerically.

Also, with the two different scales, Stan has to do more work.
Ideally, the data itself would be a bit more standardized.
> I'm actually doing it for EJ. I'm working on implementing all those models from the book.

:-) Small world, of course.

- Bob

P.S. I see you have kappa coefficients coming up next. I'd suggest
looking at something like Dawid and Skene's 1979 measurement error
model for data annotation in addition to kappa.

Vector transpose -- it turns a row vector, which is
what y[i] picks out, to a column vector (or just "vector"),
which is what multi_normal expects.

> And is it better to use col(x,j)
> instead of having array of vectors? I thought that in manual the second option was prefered.

So yes, if you made y an array of vectors, that'd be faster than
using y[i]'.

> I've also tried mu ~ normal(0,sqrt(10000)), but it's resulting in similar correlation posterior.
>

Unfortunately, all these methods can fall over in the same situations,
which typically involve highly variable scales in the posterior. What happens
is that there are sharp transitions in log posterior (for instance, when a hierarchical
variance parameter goes to zero), which are hard for all of these methods to
deal with. RMHMC will be better, but it can be slow per iteration and
limited in scalability.

I'm worried about the two versions of this model being different in Stan. If
everything else agreed other than my model, my model might be wrong. Seems
more likely than all the other ones being wrong.

> Can I ignore the warning about matrix being positive definite?

Yes, the problem arises during the simulation of the
position of the parameters under Hamiltonian dynamics.
We need to trade off the time granularity of the simulation
(step size) vs. number of steps. With smaller step size,
we get more accurate transition approximations, but it
takes more steps. This balance is tuned for optimal
sampling during warmup. The resulting balance occassionally
rejects because of too-large steps using only gradient
taking you outside of support for constrained variables
like covariance matrices.
> Or is it better to give bounds to r (-0.9999,0.9999)?

That will probably do it, but whether it's better or not is a matter
of where you think the results will be. If you get estimates near the
boundary, then you want wider bounds (closer to 0 and 1). The other
alternative is to use a stronger prior pushign values to 0.
That's why we like the LKJ priors --- you can set up a correlation matrix
that favors the identity with an adjustable strength, then use a scale
vector (i.e., the sd of the dimensions) to convert it to a correlation
matrix. So you independently control amount of shrinkage toward
identity correlation and the scales of the dimensions.
> Thanks for your time Bob.

You're welcome. The examples you've brought up have been fun and
we want to make sure Stan is usable in as many situations and for
as many kinds of models as possible.

Speaking of which, do you have plans to distribute the models when
you're done coding them? Or do a comparison with JAGS/BUGS? That'd
be fantastic, I think, for us and the BUGS and JAGS developers.
What we're interested in is for efficiency and scalability are:

(a) speed to convergence, especially from diffuse
initializations,

(b) mixing speed after convergence in terms of number
of effective samples per second, and

(c) memory use.

We're interested not only in averages, but also variation, though I'm
not so sure how to measure that other than histograms of the measurements
above. We've been finding that our chains can be pretty variable in how long they take.

- Bob

I suppose that binomial_cdf() in Stan is similar to pbinom() in R, i.e.

binomial_cdf(x, size, p) = pbinon(x, size, p) = P[X <= x]

and P[15 <= X <= 25] = P[X <= 25] - P[X < 15] = P[X <= 25] - P[X <= 14].
In R:

> p <- 0
> for (i in 15:25) p <- p + choose(50,i) * 0.4^i * (1-0.4)^(50-i)
> p
[1] 0.8887012
> pbinom(25, 50, 0.4) - pbinom(14, 50, 0.4)
[1] 0.8887012

Sergio
